name: Yohimbine mesotherapy

card.summary: Injections of the alpha-2 blocker yohimbine into fat pockets, proposed to promote local fat release for a leaner shape.
card.note: Injection mixtures are not FDA-approved for fat reduction; yohimbine has documented cardiovascular side effects.

quick.overview:
Mesotherapy is a technique of intradermal or subcutaneous injections of substances such as drugs, enzymes, vitamins and plant extracts. In body-contouring circles, mixtures containing yohimbine, an alpha-2 adrenergic blocker, are described as a way to mobilise stubborn local fat.

The appearance goal is a slimmer area such as the abdomen or thighs. Published research specifically on yohimbine mesotherapy was not found; Wikipedia's mesotherapy article says there is no conclusive research that any compound targets fat cells specifically [1][2].
quick.how: Practitioners describe small injections into the treated area in a series of sessions. Specific mixtures and amounts are not covered here.
quick.risks: Wikipedia reports that oral yohimbine can cause raised blood pressure, fast heart rate, anxiety and tremor, and interactions with prescription drugs. Mesotherapy risks include inflammation, swelling and infections, and the FDA does not control practitioners' mixtures [1][2].

lead: Yohimbine mesotherapy refers to injecting yohimbine, an alpha-2 adrenergic receptor antagonist from the bark of the yohimbe tree, into skin or subcutaneous fat as part of a mesotherapy mixture [1]. The proposed purpose is localised fat reduction for body contouring.

Mesotherapy itself involves injecting pharmaceuticals, enzymes, hormones, plant extracts or vitamins. Proponents say it induces lipolysis in fat cells; the article states there is no conclusive research showing that any compound targets fat cells specifically [2].
Yohimbine is marketed as a supplement for libido, weight loss and bodybuilding, but Wikipedia states there is virtually no published research supporting such claims [1].

chain: Alpha-2 receptor blockade in fat tissue
angle.text: Practitioners propose that blocking alpha-2 receptors in local fat promotes fat release. The idea is to trim stubborn areas without surgery.

infobox: US: unscheduled; UK: unlicensed; Canada: Rx; Australia: Schedule 4 [1]

paras: Yohimbine blocks alpha-2 adrenergic receptors and also binds some serotonin and dopamine receptors at higher concentrations. It is used in veterinary medicine to reverse xylazine sedation [1].
Mesotherapy was pioneered by Michel Pistor; the French press coined the term in 1958 and the French Academy of Medicine recognised it as a specialty in 1987 [2].

Plastic surgeon Rod Rohrich has said he knew of no data showing mesotherapy works [2]. The American Society of Plastic Surgeons has not endorsed it, and the FDA approved only deoxycholic acid (Kybella) in 2015 for submental fat [2].

Oral yohimbine at high doses can cause high blood pressure, rapid heartbeat, agitation, anxiety and tremor, and drug interactions have caused sudden low blood pressure and arrhythmia [1]. Mesotherapy has been associated with unpredictable inflammation and swelling from some ingredients, and with skin abscesses and a mycobacterial infection in an Australian salon [2].

No studies found. A small study of facial multivitamin mesotherapy found no clinically relevant rejuvenation benefit, and a pressurised mesotherapy study reported fat-layer reductions with other mixtures [2].

timeline.event: The term mesotherapy is coined by the French press [2]
French Academy of Medicine recognises it as a specialty [2]
FDA approves deoxycholic acid (Kybella) for submental fat [2]
